Engagement

Grassroots

Influencer

Integrated Communications

Return on Investment (ROI)

Unique Selling Proposition (USP)

Media Relations Terminology
Angle
The specific emphasis chosen for a story that determines the approach and perspective from which the story will be covered.
Backgrounder
An informational document often provided to the media along with a press release to give deeper insights into the context, statistics, and details about the subject matter.
Beat
The specific subject, sector, or industry that a journalist routinely covers, such as the technology beat, the healthcare beat, and so on.
Bridge
A communication technique used in interviews to transition from the interviewer’s question to a specific message that the interviewee wants to communicate.
B-roll
Supplemental or alternate footage intercut with the main shot in an interview or broadcast news story.
Byline
The line in an article that names the author of the piece.
Clip
A selected portion of a piece of media content (such as audio or video) used to demonstrate or highlight a particular point or to report on what has been broadcast or published.
Dateline
The line at the beginning of a news article that includes the date and place where the story originated.
Embargo
An agreement between sources and journalists that information provided in advance will not be published until a specific date and time.
Exclusive
A news story that is given to only one newspaper or broadcaster, potentially giving it an advantage over competitors.
Fact Sheet
A concise document providing key information on a new product, event, or other subjects, often formatted as a series of bullet points to allow for quick understanding.
Feature
A type of non-news article that provides an in-depth look at a particular topic, trend, person, or organization, often highlighting personal stories and experiences.
Flagging
Highlighting or drawing attention to a particular part of a press release or media pitch, usually to signal its importance or relevance.
Follow-up
A subsequent action where a PR professional contacts a journalist after sending a press release or pitch to ensure it was received and to gauge interest.
Gatekeeper
An individual who controls access to something, especially information or exposure in the media. Examples include a news editor or producer.
Hook
A compelling angle or piece of information that grabs the attention of journalists and their audiences.
Key Message
A core idea conveyed by an individual or organization to their target audiences, including the media, shareholders, the public, and other stakeholders.
Lead
The opening paragraph of a press release or news story that summarizes the most important points. It should include the Five Ws (who, what, when, where, why).
Media Advisory/Alert
A brief notice sent to journalists to announce an upcoming event, such as a press conference, with the goal of securing media coverage.
Media Briefing
An event where journalists are informed about the details of a particular issue or event, often including the opportunity for questions and answers.
Media Kit
A pre-packaged set of promotional materials for a person, company, or organization distributed to members of the media for promotional use, typically distributed as a digital document or web page.
Media Monitoring

The tracking of various media outlets and sources to find all relevant mentions about a company or certain topics; it can include monitoring newspapers, magazines, television, radio, and the internet.
Newsjacking
The process of injecting your ideas or angles into breaking news, in real time, in order to generate media coverage for yourself or your business.
News Hook
The element in a story that makes it newsworthy, timely, and of interest to the media and their audiences.
Off-the-Record
Information provided to a journalist that is not intended for publication. This agreement must be established prior to the information being given; otherwise, it is assumed to be on-the-record.
On Background
Part of a conversation with a journalist that can be reported on but not attributed directly to the source by name.
Op-Ed (Opinion Editorial)
An article written by someone who is not the regular staff of a publication that expresses an opinion or perspective on a current issue.
Pitch
A concise presentation of an idea for a story to a journalist or editor that outlines the main angles and benefits of the story.
Placements
The successful securing of a story, article, or mention of a person, company, or product in the media.
Press Conference
An event organized to communicate important information to multiple media outlets simultaneously, often allowing for a question-and-answer session.
Press Pool
Selected group of journalists from various media outlets who are designated to represent the wider press corps at an event due to space or security limitations.
Press Release
A written statement to the media that announces something significant or newsworthy.
Sidebar
A secondary story or information accompanying a main story, providing additional details or a different perspective.
Sound Bite
A short, catchy snippet or quote taken from a longer piece of audio or an interview that encapsulates the main point and is easy for the audience to remember.
Talking Points
Key messages designed to be emphasized by a spokesperson during an interview or media appearance.
Wire Service
A news agency that supplies syndicated news by wire to newspapers, radio, and television stations.

What Are News Values?
Journalists use several criteria to determine what constitutes news and what does not. These criteria help them assess the newsworthiness of events, stories, and information. Here are the key factors
Timeliness
News is about what is happening now or has happened recently. The more recent the event, the more newsworthy it is.
Example: A breaking news story about a natural disaster that occurred today is more newsworthy than one that happened a month ago.
Proximity
Events that occur close to the audience are more newsworthy than those that happen far away. Local news is often prioritized because it directly affects the audience.
Example: A local election in a city is more newsworthy to its residents than an election in a distant country.
Impact
The significance of an event or issue in terms of its effect on people. The greater the impact, the more newsworthy the story.
Example: A new law affecting healthcare for millions of people is more newsworthy than a minor policy change affecting a small group.
Prominence
Events involving well-known people or institutions are more newsworthy. The actions of celebrities, politicians, and public figures often attract more attention.
Example: A statement by the president is more newsworthy than a statement by a local council member.
Conflict
Stories involving conflict, tension, or controversy are often considered newsworthy. Conflict can arise from political debates, legal battles, or social issues.

Human Interest
Stories that evoke emotions, such as happiness, sadness, or curiosity, are newsworthy. These stories often focus on individuals and their experiences.
Example: A heartwarming story about a community coming together to help a family in need is newsworthy due to its emotional appeal.
Novelty
Unusual, rare, or unexpected events are newsworthy. The novelty factor makes these stories interesting and engaging.
Example: A story about a person surviving a rare medical condition or an unusual animal sighting is newsworthy due to its uniqueness.
Relevance
Stories that are relevant to the audience’s interests, concerns, and daily lives are more newsworthy. Relevance can be determined by the audience’s demographics, location, and interests.
Example: A story about rising housing prices is relevant to a community concerned about affordable living.
Currency
Some issues become newsworthy because they are currently in the public discourse. These stories gain importance due to their connection to ongoing trends or events.
Example: During a pandemic, stories related to health, vaccines, and public safety are more newsworthy.

Key Distinctions between Print and Digital Media
The differences between traditional print news and digital media are significant and impact how PR professionals approach each medium.
Traditional Print News
Format: Physical newspapers and magazines.
Publication Frequency: Often daily, weekly, or monthly.
Distribution: Limited to geographic areas where the publication is circulated.
Space Constraints: Limited space for articles, leading to more selective content.
Permanence: Once printed, content cannot be changed or updated.
Audience Engagement: Limited to letters to the editor or in-person events.
Credibility: Often perceived as more credible due to established reputations and rigorous editorial standards.
Lead Time: Longer lead times for stories due to the printing process.
Revenue Model: Primarily through subscriptions and advertising.
Digital Media
Format: Online articles, blogs, social media posts, videos, podcasts, and so on.
Publication Frequency: Continuous, with the ability to publish updates in real time.
Distribution: Global reach, accessible to anyone with an internet connection.
Space Constraints: Virtually unlimited space, allowing for more in-depth coverage and multimedia elements.
Permanence: Content can be updated, corrected, or removed at any time.
Audience Engagement: High levels of interaction through comments, shares, likes, and direct messages.
Credibility: Varies widely; some digital outlets are highly reputable, while others may lack editorial oversight.
Lead Time: Shorter lead times, allowing for rapid response to breaking news.

Media Relations Terminology
Angle
The specific emphasis chosen for a story that determines the approach and perspective from which the story will be covered.
Backgrounder
An informational document often provided to the media along with a press release to give deeper insights into the context, statistics, and details about the subject matter.
Beat
The specific subject, sector, or industry that a journalist routinely covers, such as the technology beat, the healthcare beat, and so on.
Bridge
A communication technique used in interviews to transition from the interviewer’s question to a specific message that the interviewee wants to communicate.
B-roll
Supplemental or alternate footage intercut with the main shot in an interview or broadcast news story.
Byline
The line in an article that names the author of the piece.
Clip
A selected portion of a piece of media content (such as audio or video) used to demonstrate or highlight a particular point or to report on what has been broadcast or published.
Dateline
The line at the beginning of a news article that includes the date and place where the story originated.
Embargo
An agreement between sources and journalists that information provided in advance will not be published until a specific date and time.
Exclusive
A news story that is given to only one newspaper or broadcaster, potentially giving it an advantage over competitors.
Fact Sheet
A concise document providing key information on a new product, event, or other subjects, often formatted as a series of bullet points to allow for quick understanding.
Feature
A type of non-news article that provides an in-depth look at a particular topic, trend, person, or organization, often highlighting personal stories and experiences.
Flagging
Highlighting or drawing attention to a particular part of a press release or media pitch, usually to signal its importance or relevance.
Follow-up
A subsequent action where a PR professional contacts a journalist after sending a press release or pitch to ensure it was received and to gauge interest.
Gatekeeper
An individual who controls access to something, especially information or exposure in the media. Examples include a news editor or producer.
Hook
A compelling angle or piece of information that grabs the attention of journalists and their audiences.
Key Message
A core idea conveyed by an individual or organization to their target audiences, including the media, shareholders, the public, and other stakeholders.
Lead
The opening paragraph of a press release or news story that summarizes the most important points. It should include the Five Ws (who, what, when, where, why).
Media Advisory/Alert
A brief notice sent to journalists to announce an upcoming event, such as a press conference, with the goal of securing media coverage.
Media Briefing
An event where journalists are informed about the details of a particular issue or event, often including the opportunity for questions and answers.
Media Kit
A pre-packaged set of promotional materials for a person, company, or organization distributed to members of the media for promotional use, typically distributed as a digital document or web page.
Media Monitoring

The tracking of various media outlets and sources to find all relevant mentions about a company or certain topics; it can include monitoring newspapers, magazines, television, radio, and the internet.
Newsjacking
The process of injecting your ideas or angles into breaking news, in real time, in order to generate media coverage for yourself or your business.
News Hook
The element in a story that makes it newsworthy, timely, and of interest to the media and their audiences.
Off-the-Record
Information provided to a journalist that is not intended for publication. This agreement must be established prior to the information being given; otherwise, it is assumed to be on-the-record.
On Background
Part of a conversation with a journalist that can be reported on but not attributed directly to the source by name.
Op-Ed (Opinion Editorial)
An article written by someone who is not the regular staff of a publication that expresses an opinion or perspective on a current issue.
Pitch
A concise presentation of an idea for a story to a journalist or editor that outlines the main angles and benefits of the story.
Placements
The successful securing of a story, article, or mention of a person, company, or product in the media.
Press Conference
An event organized to communicate important information to multiple media outlets simultaneously, often allowing for a question-and-answer session.
Press Pool
Selected group of journalists from various media outlets who are designated to represent the wider press corps at an event due to space or security limitations.
Press Release
A written statement to the media that announces something significant or newsworthy.
Sidebar
A secondary story or information accompanying a main story, providing additional details or a different perspective.
Sound Bite
A short, catchy snippet or quote taken from a longer piece of audio or an interview that encapsulates the main point and is easy for the audience to remember.
Talking Points
Key messages designed to be emphasized by a spokesperson during an interview or media appearance.
Wire Service
A news agency that supplies syndicated news by wire to newspapers, radio, and television stations.
